body_text: {"id":"gen-1788838004-ou3FnaLGp0TG3NSxVBHk","object":"chat.completion","created":1788838004,"model":"z-ai/glm-5.3","provider":"Together","system_fingerprint":"default","service_tier":null,"choices":[{"index":0,"logprobs":null,"finish_reason":"stop","native_finish_reason":"stop","message":{"role":"assistant","content":"{\"type\":\"finish\",\"output\":\"This analysis reconstructs the queue incident using only the synthetic evidence E01-E10. By 09:10 the queue had risen roughly 15x to 1,850 with no worker change (E02), and by 09:12 median task latency had jumped from 1.8s to 14.2s (E03). At 09:14, host resources were far from saturated: CPU 43%, memory 51%, disk 22% (E04), which argues strongly against a compute or storage bottleneck as the primary driver. The pivotal event occurred at 09:15: outbound dependency B began returning HTTP 429 for 31% of requests (E05), a classic downstream rate-limiting signature. Immediately afterward, at 09:16, retry volume increased by 420% under an exponential backoff policy capped at three retries (E06), indicating that failed calls were being re-attempted aggressively enough to multiply workload. Two natural experiments follow. First, at 09:20, doubling the worker count from 8 to 16 produced only a 6% queue reduction over ten minutes (E07). If the constraint were local processing capacity, doubling workers should have produced a near-linear throughput gain; the negligible effect confirms that workers were blocked waiting on a throttled downstream dependency, so parallelism could not help. Second, at 09:26, disabling retries for dependency B dropped queue depth 38% in six minutes (E08) at the cost of a higher direct failure rate, proving the retry policy was a significant queue amplifier. Finally, at 09:35, dependency B raised its rate limits, 429s fell below 1%, and the queue returned below 150 within eleven minutes (E09), which is the decisive causal confirmation: when the upstream constraint was removed, the system recovered without any change to our own worker count, retry code, or infrastructure. E10 rules out confounders: no deploy, schema change, restart, route change, or credential rotation occurred in the window, eliminating most internal-change hypotheses. Conclusion on primary cause: the rate limiting (HTTP 429) imposed by outbound dependency B beginning at 09:15 is the most likely primary cause of queue growth. Amplifiers: (1) the retry policy, whose 420% retry-volume increase with up to three exponential-backoff retries multiplied effective request volume against an already-throttled dependency, deepening the queue; (2) possibly fixed worker sizing, but workers are better described as blocked than as an amplifier, given E07. On the retry policy assessment: exponential backoff with a maximum of three retries is reasonable in normal conditions, but it lacked any dependency-level circuit breaker, rate-limit awareness (e.g., honoring Retry-After), or global retry budget. When 31% of calls fail, three retries per call can substantially amplify offered load; retry volume rising 420% (E06) is consistent with this. The policy is appropriate in shape but insufficient in scope for a throttling scenario. Why adding workers had limited effect: workers spend most of their time waiting on dependency B responses (including 429s and backoff sleeps). Doubling concurrency increases in-flight requests to the throttled dependency but cannot increase its granted capacity; indeed more concurrent calls can worsen throttling. The 6% improvement (E07) reflects only marginal gains from overlapping non-blocked work. Alternative hypothesis considered and rejected: an internal compute bottleneck (CPU saturation) causing slow processing. This is less supported because E04 shows CPU at only 43% during the incident, and E09 shows full recovery with zero internal changes. A second alternative, a traffic surge from clients, cannot be fully excluded because the evidence set contains no inbound request-rate metric; however, the tight temporal correlation between 429 onset (09:15) and retry surge (09:16), plus the recovery on rate-limit relief, favors the dependency-throttling explanation. Uncertainties include the absence of inbound request volume data, unknown per-request time spent in backoff sleep, whether dependency B's 429s included Retry-After headers, the baseline retry fraction before 09:15, and whether dependency B has quotas we can request increases for. Remediation should be staged: first, add dependency-level metrics (429 rate, retry rate, queue age) and alerting so throttling is detected within minutes rather than inferred from queue growth; second, implement retry hardening: honor Retry-After, add jittered backoff, cap retries at 1-2 for 429s, and add a per-dependency retry budget; third, add a circuit breaker or client-side rate limiter that matches dependency B's allowance so we self-throttle below their limit rather than triggering 429s; fourth, open an operational relationship with dependency B's owners to negotiate quota, get advance notice of limit changes, and establish an escalation path (E09 shows limits can be raised); fifth, validate queue back-pressure behavior: define what the system does when the queue exceeds a threshold (shed, defer, or degrade) instead of accumulating 1,850 items; sixth, run a controlled load test reproducing a 31% 429 scenario to verify the circuit breaker and retry budget prevent queue growth, and document a runbook that includes the proven emergency lever from E08 (temporarily disabling retries) with its known trade-off of increased direct failures. In summary, the evidence triangulates cleanly: onset (E05), amplification (E06), insensitivity to local scaling (E07), sensitivity to retry removal (E08), and resolution upon upstream relief (E09), with confounders excluded (E10). Primary cause: external rate limiting by dependency B. Primary amplifier: retry policy without rate-limit awareness.
